topic: Transformer/HV equipment supply, lead times, and whether orphaned production slots actually exist (as of mid-November 2026)

findings.question: What are current lead times for large power transformers (LPTs), generator step-up units (GSUs), and HV circuit breakers/switchgear?
findings.answer: Still at multi-year highs and, at the GSU end, STILL LENGTHENING — not easing. The most-cited primary dataset is Wood Mackenzie's supply-chain survey (via Reuters): LPTs ~128 weeks (Q2 2025 survey), GSUs ~144 weeks in that same survey rising above 160 weeks in Q1 2026 (from 143 weeks average in 2024), and HV circuit breakers ~125 weeks in H2 2025, up from 77 weeks in 2023. PwC analysts put the largest units at up to four years. HV switchgear is the weakest-sourced class: vendor trackers disagree wildly (34–46 weeks in one distributor report vs 125 weeks for custom HV breaker configurations; MV switchgear ~44 weeks on a WoodMac-derived index, 40–80 weeks across other surveys, 78–104 weeks for 38 kV class). Distribution-class units (10–50 MVA, pad-mount) are the only segment with credible easing, around 40–78 weeks vs 2023 peaks. CAUTION: the single-digit-week HV switchgear figures and the widely circulated '+100% transformers / +260% GSU' percentages do not appear in the Reuters/WoodMac originals; I could not reach woodmac.com (DNS blocked in this session's network allowlist), so all WoodMac figures here are via syndication, not the primary report.
findings.figures: LPT ~128 weeks (WoodMac Q2 2025 survey). GSU >160 weeks Q1 2026, up from 143 wks avg 2024 and ~144 wks in Q2 2025 survey. HV circuit breakers ~125 weeks H2 2025, up from 77 weeks 2023. Largest LPTs up to 48 months (PwC). Distribution 40–78 weeks. HV switchgear: 34–46 wks to 125 wks depending on source (unresolved). WoodMac estimated power-transformer supply shortfall narrowed from 30% (2025) to 15% (2026).
findings.as_of: GSU/LPT: Q1 2026 (WoodMac via Reuters); HV breakers: H2 2025 — the breaker number is ~12 months stale and should be re-quoted before use

findings.question: How deep are OEM order books, and are OEMs 'sold out' through a specific year?
findings.answer: Backlogs are at record highs and company-reported, but the specific claim 'transformer capacity is sold out through 2029/2030' is NOT established from any company disclosure — it is analyst/commentary characterization, and the clearest 'sold out' evidence is for GAS TURBINES, not transformers. Company-reported: Hitachi Energy FY2025 orders ~$32.8bn against a $57.9bn backlog (revenue $19.8bn, +26%); Hitachi's wider Energy business $66.4bn (JPY 10.5tn) backlog at end-September 2026; Siemens Energy Grid Technologies a record EUR 51bn (~$59bn) backlog as of 5 August 2026; GE Vernova Electrification backlog $42.2bn at end-September 2026 (including $5bn at Prolec GE). The turbine side is where capacity is explicitly committed: GE Vernova large-frame capacity reported fully sold through 2028 with 70%+ booked for 2029, and 116 GW of gas position at June 2026 (53 GW firm equipment backlog + 63 GW slot reservations). For transformers, implied delivery windows come from a single commercial tracker (Hitachi 48–60 months, GE Vernova 60+ months, Siemens 'backlog through 2030') that conflicts with other sources.
findings.figures: Hitachi Energy: $32.8bn FY2025 orders, $57.9bn backlog, $19.8bn revenue (+26%); Hitachi Energy segment $66.4bn backlog (Sept 2026). Siemens Energy Grid Technologies: EUR 51bn record backlog (5 Aug 2026). GE Vernova Electrification: $42.2bn backlog (Sept 2026), incl. $5bn Prolec GE. GE Vernova gas: 116 GW = 53 GW backlog + 63 GW slot reservations (June 2026); 24 GW/yr target 2028, 30 GW/yr 2030.
findings.as_of: Backlogs: Aug–Sept 2026 (current). 'Sold out through 2029/2030' for transformers: not-established.

findings.question: What capacity expansions come online 2027–2029, and are they easing lead times?
findings.answer: Large, real, and specifically dated — but almost none of it lands before 2028, and the available evidence says new plants do NOT shorten lead times inside the current procurement horizon. Announced: Hitachi Energy South Boston, Virginia $457m LPT plant (groundbreaking June 2026, to be the largest US LPT plant, 825 jobs, ~2028); Hitachi Energy Gallman, Mississippi $528m (announced Sept 2026, more than doubles Crystal Springs capacity, production begins 2029); Hitachi Energy Alamo, Tennessee $106m (components); Hitachi Energy Varennes, Quebec +CAD 270m/$195m LPT (Oct 2025); Siemens Energy Charlotte, North Carolina $150m — its FIRST US LPT plant, production expected early 2027; Prolec GE Goldsboro, North Carolina ~$140–150m, doubling medium-power output to ~420 units/yr (+~200 units/yr), part of >$300m across sites; Eaton three-phase transformer plant in South Carolina targeting 2027. Industry total: nearly $2bn committed to new/expanded US transformer capacity since 2023, plus DOE program reportedly up to $375m. Offshore: Hitachi Karjan, Gujarat ~$214m (INR 2,000 crore) completing FY2028; Siemens Energy India ~$220m (INR 2,060 crore) adding 30,000 MVA, operational 2030–2032. The honest read is a plateau with partial easing in distribution only: an October 2026 industry update states no announced domestic capacity arrives before 2028 and that new plants do not translate into shorter lead times within the current procurement horizon.
findings.figures: US: Hitachi South Boston VA $457m (~2028); Hitachi Gallman MS $528m (production 2029); Hitachi Alamo TN $106m; Hitachi Varennes QC CAD 270m; Siemens Charlotte NC $150m (early 2027); Prolec GE Goldsboro NC ~$140–150m, 420 units/yr; Eaton SC (2027). ~$2bn committed since 2023; DOE up to $375m. India: Hitachi Karjan INR 2,000cr (FY2028); Siemens Energy India INR 2,060cr / 30,000 MVA (2030–32). Siemens Energy global transformer capacity +~50% by 2030.
findings.as_of: November 2026 (announcements current; Hitachi MS announced Sept 2026)

findings.question: What are tariff effects on imported transformers in 2026?
findings.answer: Material but genuinely unresolved at the rate level — sources contradict each other and I would NOT put a specific percentage in a business plan without checking CBP/Federal Register directly. What is reasonably consistent: a 2 April 2026 proclamation replaced the flat 50% metals tariff with a tiered Section 232 system effective 6 April, and duties now apply to the FULL customs value of covered metal articles and derivatives rather than only the declared metal content — a significant escalation for assembled equipment. A 1 June 2026 proclamation adjusted the regimes again, effective 8 June 2026 through 31 December 2027, with a US-origin test (85% by weight since 8 June 2026) qualifying some imports for a 10% rate. On transformer rates themselves, sources conflict: one says distribution transformers carry a 25% base rate and switchgear assemblies are not on the June 2026 lists; another says a 15% reduced rate reaches two whole-transformer HTS lines, 8504.23.00 (liquid dielectric >10,000 kVA) and 8504.34.00 (non-liquid >500 kVA). GOES sits in the highest tier, put at 50% by one source. On 6 August 2026 Commerce proposed adding 14 further derivative categories; no implementing notice found. Verify against CBP CSMS #68253075 and #68855869.
findings.figures: 2 Apr 2026 proclamation, effective 6 Apr: tiered rates, full customs value. 1 Jun 2026 proclamation effective 8 Jun 2026–31 Dec 2027; 85%-by-weight US-origin test for a 10% rate. Transformer rates disputed: 25% base (one source) vs 15% reduced on HTS 8504.23.00 and 8504.34.00 (another). GOES highest tier, up to 50%. Copper tariffs up to 50%. 6 Aug 2026: 14 proposed additional derivative categories, not implemented.
findings.as_of: June–August 2026 rules; rate specifics contested as of Nov 2026

findings.question: How much have transformer prices inflated since 2020?
findings.answer: Roughly a doubling, and still rising as of September 2026 — this is one of the better-supported facts in the whole topic. Wood Mackenzie's earlier published figure was 60–80% above January 2020 levels, later raised to 70–75%+. The most recent and most independent anchor is the BLS producer price index for transformer manufacturing: +7.8% year-on-year to September 2026 and ~86% above its January 2020 level (a separate re-basing puts it +91.4% as of July 2026). Component-level attribution (via WoodMac): power transformers +77%, GSUs +45%, distribution +45–95% vs 2019. Input drivers: GOES has roughly doubled since January 2020 and copper is up ~50%, with ~95% of domestic GOES reportedly from a single supplier. Note that producer-price indices are not project quotes and do not translate directly into cost per MVA — I could not source a credible per-MVA benchmark.
findings.figures: BLS transformer manufacturing PPI: +7.8% YoY to Sept 2026, ~+86% vs Jan 2020 (also cited +91.4% as of Jul 2026). WoodMac: +60–80% vs Jan 2020, later 70–75%+. By class vs 2019: power transformers +77%, GSU +45%, distribution +45–95%. GOES ~2x since Jan 2020; copper ~+50%. ~95% of US GOES from one supplier. No per-MVA benchmark established.
findings.as_of: September 2026 (PPI) — current

findings.question: THE CRITICAL QUESTION, PART A: Do orphaned/cancelled NEW transformers actually exist and change hands?
findings.answer: YES — the market for orphaned PHYSICAL UNITS is real, is already intermediated by named brokers, and has live new/unused inventory. This is the single most important positive finding, and it is also the finding that most constrains the business, because the intermediaries already exist. Live examples found: surplustransformers.com explicitly buys and sells new, unused transformers from cancelled generation projects, with GSU/step-up units listed as available; Transformer Exchange runs a dedicated 'New Unused Inventory' page listing e.g. a 2025 Toshiba 90/112/140 MVA 138/34.5 kV LTC unit and a 400 MVA GSU, and states that units under five years old may carry a TRANSFERABLE WARRANTY; CTG Power Systems lists specific never-energized units including a 2025 Georgia Transformer 66/88/110 MVA stored in the USA, three 'NEW' Prolec-GE 30/40/50/56 MVA units and a Toshiba 90/112/140 MVA step-up; J&J Transformers (Sugar Land, TX) buys/sells new, unused and cancelled-project units 69–500 kV and will take them at ANY stage — engineering, in-manufacture, post-FAT, delivered, stored, or installed-but-never-energized — provided ownership and transfer rights are documented. A primary-source cancellation exists: an Indo Tech Transformers filing to the Bombay Stock Exchange (11 March 2026) disclosed a renewable developer cancelling an order for six 220 kV transformers worth ~INR 64.99 crore due to project delay; the filing does not say what happened to the slot. On pricing, one guide estimates new-surplus units transact at 70–90% of new cost and attributes supply to OEM and distributor cancellations and overbuilds — that is the vendor's own estimate, not market data. What is NOT established: volume, turnover, liquidity, or clearing prices. Every inventory page is a marketing page; none of the listings were independently verified, and availability on these sites requires written confirmation.
findings.figures: Four named active intermediaries: surplustransformers.com, transformerexchange.com, ctgpowersystems.com, jjtransformers.co. J&J range 69–500 kV, accepts units at 6 lifecycle stages. Specific listed units: 2025 Toshiba 90/112/140 MVA 138/34.5 kV LTC; 400 MVA GSU; 2025 Georgia Transformer 66/88/110 MVA; 3x NEW Prolec-GE 30/40/50/56 MVA. Transferable OEM warranty possible if unit <5 years old. New-surplus pricing estimated at 70–90% of new (vendor estimate). Primary cancellation: 6x 220 kV units, INR 64.99 crore, disclosed 11 Mar 2026. Market size/turnover: not established.
findings.as_of: November 2026 for broker listings; 11 March 2026 for the Indo Tech filing

findings.question: THE CRITICAL QUESTION, PART B: Do production SLOTS / order positions themselves change hands between buyers — i.e. is there a tradable slot, as opposed to a tradable transformer?
findings.answer: NOT ESTABLISHED — and this is the finding that should most worry the business. Across four separate searches I found NO source describing an OEM-sanctioned mechanism, exchange, or completed transaction in which a cancelled transformer order's factory position was reassigned or resold to a third-party buyer. What exists is adjacent but different in a way that matters: (1) slots are bought FROM OEMs, not between buyers — Reuters Events reporting (via pv magazine, 11 May 2026) says some firms are now purchasing production slots at a premium before they have even finalized a specific project site, which is primary-market pre-buying; (2) the formal slot-reservation instrument is real but gas-turbine, not transformer — GE Vernova reports slot reservation agreements separately from backlog (63 GW SRAs vs 53 GW equipment backlog at June 2026), converted 6 GW of SRAs to orders in Q1 2026 and 3 GW in Q2 2025, and its 10-K warns counterparties 'may not place orders equal to the value of their reservation amount or at all' — yet nothing I found discloses whether an SRA is transferable or what happens to the deposit on cancellation; (3) analogue reservation agreements in other industries routinely BAR buyer assignment without the seller's written consent while letting the seller assign freely, and several explicitly state the reservation does not guarantee a production slot or delivery date; (4) the underlying asset appears unstable even for the original holder — distributor commentary reports manufacturers shifting slots by 6–9 months mid-build, so a signed order does not fix a delivery date. The closest thing to slot trading that is actually evidenced is J&J Transformers accepting units still at the engineering or in-manufacture stage subject to documented transfer rights — which is de facto assignment of an in-progress order, mediated by a broker, one unit at a time, with the OEM's consent as the gating item. Plainly: the physical orphan exists; the tradable slot as a financial instrument does not, on this evidence.
findings.figures: Zero sources found describing an OEM-run or third-party slot/order-position exchange for transformers. GE Vernova (gas, not transformers): 63 GW slot reservations vs 53 GW equipment backlog at June 2026; 6 GW SRA-to-order conversion in Q1 2026, 3 GW in Q2 2025; transferability and cancellation terms not disclosed. Reuters Events (11 May 2026): firms buying slots at a premium pre-site. OEMs reported shifting slots 6–9 months mid-build. Analogue agreements: buyer assignment requires seller written consent; seller may assign freely; reservation does not lock a slot or date.
findings.as_of: November 2026 — searched specifically and repeatedly; absence of evidence after targeted search, not merely unsearched

findings.question: Do OEMs require non-refundable deposits that make cancellation costly (and therefore suppress the supply of orphaned slots)?
findings.answer: Probably yes, and substantially — but the transformer-specific numbers are poorly sourced. For gas turbines the pattern is reasonably evidenced: a deposit of roughly 20% of turbine price to hold a slot, non-refundable, with final price not necessarily locked at reservation; GE Vernova's 10-Q ties a large cash inflow to down payments on orders and slot reservation agreements at Power. For transformers the only figure found is a supplier-side claim of 20–40% upfront non-refundable deposits with cancellation triggering deposit forfeiture plus liability for committed raw materials — this comes from a slide deck with no clear provenance and should be treated as unverified. The structural inference matters more than the number: large non-refundable deposits mean a cancelling buyer's rational move is to take delivery and resell the physical unit (recovering 70–90% of new per the surplus brokers) rather than walk away and forfeit 20–40%. That is consistent with what the evidence actually shows — a market in orphaned physical units — and inconsistent with a liquid market in abandoned slots.
findings.figures: Gas turbines: ~20% of price, non-refundable, to hold a slot; one documented case of a non-refundable deposit payable in 2026 with price still to be negotiated. Transformers: 20–40% upfront non-refundable claimed by one unverified source, plus raw-material liability on cancellation. GE Vernova cash inflow attributed to down payments on orders and SRAs (10-Q).
findings.as_of: 2026; transformer-specific deposit terms require verification against actual OEM contracts

findings.question: Are buyers speculatively over-ordering transformers (phantom demand), which would create a future wave of orphaned equipment?
findings.answer: Phantom demand is real and large — but it sits in the INTERCONNECTION QUEUE, not demonstrably in equipment orders, and that distinction kills the simplest version of the orphaned-slot thesis. Queue phantom demand: US data centre developers have requested ~1,066 GW of grid connections while Wood Mackenzie expects utilities to commit to only ~28%; another analysis puts only 23% of disclosed requests in a high-confidence category; one utility's high-probability load fell from 18 GW to 11 GW once binding financial commitments were required. Project attrition is also real: Bloomberg citing Sightline Climate reports nearly half of US data centre capacity planned for 2026 faces delay or cancellation, with only 5 GW under construction against 16 GW planned, and one tracker counts 20+ cancellations in Q1 2026 representing $41.7bn and 3.5+ GW (unverified). BUT: I found no evidence that utilities or developers are placing duplicate or speculative TRANSFORMER orders. What the reporting shows instead is utilities buying genuinely early because of scarcity — ordering equipment for projects known five years ahead — and building financial machinery to hold it, e.g. Duke Energy setting up procurement subsidiaries using specialised financing and leasing structures. Over-ordering is discussed in the sources as a forward-looking tail risk of committing to single-source factory slots in 2026, not as an observed behaviour. Note the asymmetry: most cancelled data centres are cancelled BEFORE a transformer order is placed, because the equipment order is the expensive, deposit-bearing commitment that developers avoid until the project is real.
findings.figures: 1,066 GW of US data centre interconnection requests; WoodMac expects ~28% to be committed; 23% high-confidence in another analysis; one utility 18 GW → 11 GW after binding commitments. Sightline Climate/Bloomberg: ~half of 2026-planned US DC capacity delayed or cancelled; 5 GW under construction vs 16 GW planned. 20+ cancellations Q1 2026, $41.7bn, 3.5+ GW (unverified). Utilities ordering ~5 years ahead. Duplicate transformer ordering: no evidence found.
findings.as_of: Q3–Q4 2026 for queue data; Q1 2026 for cancellation tracker

implication_for_business: The scarcity premise holds; the inventory premise half-holds; the specific product you were going to sell does not exist yet and may not be legally constructible. Taking those in order. (1) Scarcity is real, durable and well sourced: GSUs above 160 weeks and still lengthening as of Q1 2026, HV breakers ~125 weeks, prices ~86% above January 2020 and still rising at 7.8% YoY to September 2026, record OEM backlogs, and essentially no new US capacity landing before 2028 — Siemens Charlotte in early 2027 is the first, Hitachi Mississippi not until 2029. Demand for time-to-power intermediation is not the question. (2) Orphaned PHYSICAL units exist and already trade. Four named brokers — Surplus Transformers, Transformer Exchange, CTG Power Systems, J&J Transformers — carry live new/unused and never-energized inventory up to 400 MVA GSU class, reportedly at 70–90% of new, sometimes with transferable OEM warranty under five years. This is the strongest finding and it is double-edged: it validates the need and simultaneously means you are entering an occupied, broker-mediated niche, not an empty one. Your edge cannot be 'a marketplace exists now'; it has to be price discovery, verification (serial numbers, FAT reports, title) and matching speed, because the incumbents are opaque single-dealer inventory pages, not exchanges. (3) The core thesis — that cancelled PRODUCTION SLOTS are an orphaned asset class that can be cleared on an exchange — is NOT established. I searched for it four ways and found no OEM-sanctioned reassignment mechanism, no completed slot-resale transaction, and no third party trading transformer order positions. Slots are bought from OEMs at a premium pre-site (Reuters Events, May 2026), which is primary-market pre-buying, not secondary trading. The one formally disclosed slot instrument is GE Vernova's gas-turbine SRA, 63 GW of it, and even there transferability and cancellation terms are undisclosed. Analogue reservation contracts bar buyer assignment without seller consent while letting the seller assign freely, and OEMs reportedly shift slots 6–9 months mid-build — so the underlying asset is both non-transferable by default and unstable in date. (4) The economics explain the absence rather than contradicting it. With 20–40% non-refundable deposits plus raw-material liability, a cancelling buyer's rational move is to take delivery and resell the steel at 70–90% of new, not to abandon the slot. And most phantom data centres die before the transformer order is placed, because that order IS the expensive commitment. So the supply of truly abandoned slots is structurally thin, which is exactly what the search results show. Three consequences for the plan. First, reposition from slot exchange to orphaned-unit exchange plus verified title/spec diligence — that inventory is proven to exist. Second, treat OEM consent as the product's gating dependency, not a detail: if the business is to broker in-progress order positions (J&J demonstrably does this unit-by-unit, subject to documented transfer rights), the plan needs at least one OEM's written assignment terms before it can be underwritten, and nobody has published them. Third, the honest diligence conclusion is that one load-bearing assumption from the original research is unverified: nobody checked whether slots change hands, and on targeted search they do not appear to. Before committing capital, get an actual OEM master supply agreement and a broker's transaction log; and note that woodmac.com is blocked in this session's network settings, so every Wood Mackenzie lead-time and price figure here is syndicated rather than primary and should be re-sourced from the report itself.

topic: Who already does this: transformer/grid-equipment marketplaces, procurement advisory firms, and forward/slot-market analogues from adjacent capacity-scarce industries

findings.question: What does Anza Exchange actually transact — new vs used, transformers and breakers, slots or physical units — and what is Anza Renewables' funding and scale?
findings.answer: Anza Exchange is a B2B LISTINGS marketplace for NEW equipment: power transformers, HV breakers and solar modules, positioned on shorter lead times and better pricing than ordering direct. Search and posting listings were free at launch, with registration required; early material indicates HV breakers were initially accepted as listings only rather than fully transactable. Crucially for our thesis: it lists physical new units, NOT production slots or order positions — nothing in the sourced material suggests it transacts an order position. Parent Anza Renewables is a solar/storage procurement-analytics business (PitchBook: founded 2021, ~86 employees), investors Angeleno Group and Energy Capital Partners, with its latest deal classified by PitchBook as a buyout/LBO. The Munich Re Ventures hypothesis is WRONG — Anza does not appear in MRV's portfolio listings. NOT ESTABLISHED: Exchange launch date, listing counts, GMV, fee/take-rate schedule, Exchange-specific revenue, and whether breakers are fully supported. Caveat on method: a direct fetch of exchange.anzarenewables.com was blocked by this session's network policy, so all of the above is search-snippet derived and must be verified on-site before it goes into a plan. Separately, Anza publishes substantive transformer/breaker market commentary — meaning it is also competing for the advisory/thought-leadership position, not just the listings position.
findings.figures: Founded 2021; ~86 employees; 3 product categories (new power transformers, HV breakers, solar modules); $0 search/listing fee at launch; 2 named investors (Angeleno Group, Energy Capital Partners); latest deal type buyout/LBO; 0 sourced figures for listings, GMV, take rate or Exchange revenue
findings.as_of: Site content as of Nov 2026; PitchBook/Crunchbase profile fields are undated and the employee count and investor list may be stale

findings.question: Who are the incumbent used/surplus transformer and grid-equipment venues, what scale do they operate at, and does MegaGrid Supply exist?
findings.answer: Four live venues, all classic listings/dealer businesses in PHYSICAL units — none is an exchange and none trades order positions. (1) Surplus Record: the largest and oldest, directory-style, with 4,469 listings in the 60Hz three-phase transformer category alone; it publicly reports more than 5,000 transformer inquiries over the past year and attributes the surge to new-build lead times of 18-24 months or longer. Revenue is dealer subscriptions/listings, not transaction take. (2) Transformer Exchange Inc (transformerexchange.com), Traverse City, Michigan — a Surplus Record dealer since 2008 that sells, rents and buys used, reconditioned and new transformers including mobile substations and HV; sample live inventory: a 336 MVA 230/15.5kV GE (2012) GSU at $850,000 prepped, tested and loaded with a 230kV breaker included, and a 54/72/90 MVA 115kV/34.5kV Siemens (2025) with original warranty. This is a principal taking title, not a platform. (3) Utility Surplus Exchange — connects utilities and contractors across power & distribution transformers, switchgear, voltage regulators, circuit breakers, reclosers and capacitor banks. (4) Electrical Trader — new/used/surplus aimed at electricians, contractors and facility managers, so a lower-voltage/commercial skew rather than HV. MegaGrid Supply: NOT ESTABLISHED — zero pages returned; it may not exist, may be renamed, or may be too new/small to index. Structural read: the incumbent set monetises attention (listings/subscriptions) or inventory (dealing), and nobody in it monetises the transaction or the time dimension.
findings.figures: Surplus Record: 4,469 listings in one transformer category; >5,000 transformer inquiries in trailing year; cites 18-24+ month new-build lead times. Transformer Exchange: dealer since 2008; example asset $850,000 for 336 MVA 230/15.5kV GSU incl. 230kV breaker. Utility Surplus Exchange: 6+ equipment categories, 5 MVA substation transformer on homepage. MegaGrid Supply: 0 search results
findings.as_of: Listing pages Nov 2026; Surplus Record demand release 2026

findings.question: How large is the scarcity this business would arbitrage, is it widening or closing, and what policy sits over it?
findings.answer: The scarcity is real and large but the sources disagree on magnitude, and there is credible counter-evidence that it is a window, not a permanent condition. Lead times: Wood Mackenzie's 2026 survey puts substation transformers above 160 weeks and GSUs at ~144 weeks; POWER Magazine says 2-3 years for power transformers and GSUs; Reuters (via Kitco, 11 May 2026) reports queues up to 4 years for some high-capacity units citing PwC, with transformer prices up ~80% over five years; a September 2026 Reuters report says some equipment orders now stretch 3-5 years out, with utilities bidding directly against data-centre developers for the same hardware pool. Switchgear is a parallel binding constraint: Terrapin's June 2026 data gives 15kV-class MV switchgear at 52-80 weeks, 38kV at 78-104 weeks and pad-mount transformers at 40-65 weeks, against roughly 24 weeks pre-pandemic. COUNTER-EVIDENCE, and material to terminal value: Rystad expects nearly 200 GVA of new transformer manufacturing capacity to come online in 2026 — so underwrite the arbitrage as a 3-5 year window rather than a structural condition. POLICY OVERHANG, flagged as single-source and UNVERIFIED: Anza's commentary describes Executive Order 14421 of 26 August 2026 declaring an IEEPA national emergency over foreign-produced bulk-power equipment (transformers, inverters, battery storage systems, circuit breakers and related components), with DOE implementing rules due 24 December 2026. Verify against the Federal Register before using it — but if accurate it both constrains what is tradable (foreign-origin units and slots) and creates a provenance/origin-compliance service line.
findings.figures: >160 weeks substation transformer and ~144 weeks GSU (Wood Mackenzie 2026); 2-3 years (POWER); up to 4 years (PwC via Reuters, 11 May 2026); 3-5 years (Reuters, Sept 2026); transformer prices +80% over 5 years; MV switchgear 52-80 weeks (15kV) and 78-104 weeks (38kV) vs ~24 weeks pre-pandemic; pad-mount transformers 40-65 weeks; ~200 GVA new transformer manufacturing capacity due online in 2026 (Rystad); EO 14421 dated 26 Aug 2026 with DOE rules due 24 Dec 2026 (unverified, single relayed source)
findings.as_of: Lead-time and price data May-Sept 2026; Rystad outlook 2026; EO 14421 claim Aug/Dec 2026 and NOT independently verified

findings.question: Do transformer and power-equipment production slots already exist as a contractual instrument, and is anyone reselling them?
findings.answer: Yes on the primary side, with real commercial substance — and no observable secondary market. PRIMARY: GE Vernova uses the explicit term 'slot reservation agreements'. In Q1 2026 it signed 21 GW of new gas equipment agreements of which only 2 GW were firm orders and 19 GW were reservations; its reserved slot book reportedly rose from 43 GW to 56 GW in a single quarter. For transformers, GE Vernova indicated at a conference (reported by Asia Business Daily, 14 April 2026) that slot reservations are 'already secured through 2031'. Commercial terms: manufacturers typically hold a slot for 10-30% of equipment cost, deposits are commonly non-refundable and forfeited if the buyer walks, and going without a reservation adds roughly 8-16 weeks. Developers are reported to buy slots years in advance — sometimes with no specific project attached — and to use the reservation as a hedge against raw-material, FX and wage inflation over a multi-year contract. That last behaviour is the strongest demand signal for our business: buyers are already holding slots speculatively and therefore already hold positions they may want to exit. SECONDARY: across 14 searches I found NO source describing a slot or order position changing hands, and no venue quoting slots. Where the sector says 'secondary market' it means used or surplus physical units. One analysis warns explicitly that secondary inventory cannot be relied on with the same certainty as a contracted manufacturing slot and should be treated as an option to activate when a suitable unit appears. Read the absence as absence of evidence and as white space, not as proof: bilateral private novations very plausibly already happen and would be invisible to search.
findings.figures: GE Vernova Q1 2026: 21 GW agreements signed, 2 GW firm, 19 GW reservations; reserved book 43 GW to 56 GW in one quarter; transformer slots booked through 2031. Slot deposits 10-30% of equipment cost, typically non-refundable; +8-16 weeks lead time without a reservation. 0 sourced instances of a slot or order position being resold; 0 venues quoting slots
findings.as_of: Q1 2026 GE Vernova figures; Asia Business Daily 14 Apr 2026; Terrapin June 2026. The negative finding on resale reflects 14 searches as of 16 Nov 2026

findings.question: Can a transformer order position legally be transferred at all — i.e. can a slot be a tradable instrument?
findings.answer: Only with the manufacturer's written consent, which is discretionary and priced. This is the single most load-bearing constraint on the entire business and it should be the first page of the plan. Hard evidence from actual purchase-order terms: Virginia Transformer Corp's standard terms treat an assignment made without prior written approval as VOID, and an older VTC sales form required a $10,000 assignment fee to be paid before any assignment would be granted while expressly reserving the seller's right to deny any assignment request outright. WC Magnetics' PO terms state that no assignment of rights — specifically including rights to money due — and no delegation of duties binds the counterparty until written consent is given. Mechanically, moving a slot to a new buyer is a NOVATION (substituting the party and releasing the original from liability), not a mere assignment of rights, so the OEM's written consent is required by definition; in New York a novation must state on its face that it is one. Consequence: a transformer slot cannot be a bearer instrument, cannot be cleared, and cannot be anonymously matched. It can only be a consented novation that the OEM blesses — which makes the OEM, not the two counterparties, the gatekeeper and the pricing power. NOT ESTABLISHED, and these are the first three diligence questions: whether the HV majors (Hitachi Energy, Siemens Energy, GE Vernova, Prolec GE, WEG) permit assignment and on what terms; whether a resale premium above original contract price is enforceable or must be shared with the OEM; and the tax treatment of a transferred deposit. Note the generalisation risk — the two PO forms examined are mid-size/specialty manufacturers, not the HV majors, so extending their terms to the majors is INFERRED, not sourced.
findings.figures: $10,000 assignment fee required before assignment granted (Virginia Transformer, older sales form), with seller's right to deny reserved; unapproved assignment = void; 2 of 2 PO forms examined require written consent for any transfer; 0 of 5 major HV OEM assignment regimes established
findings.as_of: VTC terms rev. 2025-05 and 2022-11; WC Magnetics terms undated — possibly stale, re-pull current versions

findings.question: Who sells equipment procurement advisory and expediting into data centres and IPPs, and do owner's-engineer firms run procurement desks?
findings.answer: Weakly established — and the thinness of the competitive map is itself a finding. What I could source: Burns & McDonnell markets specialised experience in long-lead equipment procurement, utility interconnection and phased EPC substation delivery, and delivers data-centre substations as EPC (its Temple Data Center project in Texas added a 138-34kV substation with lines to switchgear, transformers and switchboards, phased so the tenant could install and test as each section completed). Its in-house consultancy 1898 & Co. provides business, technology and security consulting and handles transmission planning and power-systems studies for data-centre work — so procurement sits inside an EPC/OE relationship rather than being sold as a standalone product. Separately, Terrapin Construction Group publishes switchgear/transformer/generator lead-time indices as procurement-services marketing, and Archdesk publishes long-lead-equipment management guidance the same way — i.e. lead-time intelligence is already being used as lead-gen content by construction and software firms, which means our information product has no moat on its own. NOT ESTABLISHED: any named pure-play transformer expediting firm; the procurement-desk offerings of Black & Veatch, Sargent & Lundy, POWER Engineers or Leidos; fee structures (percentage of equipment value vs retainer vs day rate); market share; and whether any owner's engineer takes principal positions in equipment. The apparent absence of a pure-play expediting competitor is encouraging but 14 searches is not a market map — this needs a dedicated research pass plus practitioner interviews before it goes in a plan as white space.
findings.figures: 1 named firm with explicit long-lead-equipment procurement positioning (Burns & McDonnell, with 1898 & Co. as its consulting arm); 1 construction firm publishing lead-time indices as marketing (Terrapin, June 2026); 1 example data-centre substation scope (138-34kV, phased); 0 fee schedules sourced; 0 of 4 other major OE firms' procurement offerings established; 0 pure-play expediting firms identified
findings.as_of: Burns & McDonnell pages undated; UK piece 11 Dec 2025 (possibly stale); Terrapin data June 2026

findings.question: Semiconductor analogue: does a reserved-capacity instrument work, how is it structured, and does it trade?
findings.answer: It works extremely well as a bilateral balance-sheet instrument — and after 25+ years it still does not trade. That combination is the most important lesson for us. STRUCTURE: Cirrus Logic's 2021 capacity reservation agreement with GlobalFoundries covering 2022-2026 comprised a $60m NON-REFUNDABLE reservation fee amortised over the term plus a $195m prepayment for future wafers credited back against purchases, with shortfall payments if committed quantities were not bought. By 31 March 2026 the reservation-fee balance had amortised down to $6.7m and the prepayment balance to $14.7m — the instrument wound down exactly as designed, auditable in SEC filings throughout. It scales down too: GCT Semiconductor disclosed on its 13 November 2026 Q3 call a $7m prepayment to a foundry to preserve wafer capacity, reportedly securing production into 1H 2027. ECONOMICS: Squire Patton Boggs notes these deals impose take-or-pay or prepayment obligations fixing volumes or reserved capacity in advance; the buyer carries the downside in a softening market while the seller resists overcommitting capacity to a single customer — the same two-sided risk a transformer slot carries. PRECEDENT DEPTH: the structure dates to at least 1998-2000, when C-Cube and Oak Technology filings describe foundry deposits and loans exchanged for guaranteed capacity, with unused deposits forfeitable if purchase levels were missed. TRANSFERABILITY: NOT ESTABLISHED — no source found addressing assignment or resale of a wafer CRA. The inference is strong: the blocker is not instrument design (these are financeable, amortisable and audited) but non-fungibility — each contract is bespoke to a process node, a customer qualification and a counterparty relationship, so there is nothing to standardise into a traded contract.
findings.figures: Cirrus Logic/GlobalFoundries 2021 CRA covering 2022-2026: $60m non-refundable reservation fee + $195m prepayment; balances $6.7m and $14.7m respectively at 31 Mar 2026. GCT Semiconductor: $7m foundry prepayment securing capacity into 1H 2027 (disclosed 13 Nov 2026). Precedent depth ~26 years (1998 Oak Technology to 2026). 0 sourced instances of a wafer CRA being assigned or traded
findings.as_of: Cirrus FY2026 report, balances as of 31 Mar 2026; GCT call 13 Nov 2026

findings.question: Maritime analogues: how do ocean-freight slot charters and shipbuilding berth slots actually work, what makes them work, and what blocks them?
findings.answer: Ocean slot charter is the one genuinely working slot market, and its enabling conditions are precisely the ones a transformer market lacks. WHAT MAKES IT WORK: (a) the unit is standardised and fungible — a defined number of TEU slots on a named voyage at a set price per slot; ZIM/CSCL's FMC-filed agreement sets round-voyage allocations in TEU per trade. (b) Counterparties are peers in a repeated game: carriers both buy and sell capacity, so cross-alliance deals are proliferating (ONE and Evergreen filed a transpacific slot-exchange agreement with the FMC; Maersk/Hamburg Süd; BAL/Transfar on an 'as needed, as available' basis), with lines now putting capacity ahead of customer-retention risk. (c) A public filing regime (the US Federal Maritime Commission) makes terms visible and gives antitrust comfort. (d) Where pricing is contentious, some lines prefer 'used or not used' capacity-exchange agreements that dispense with rate setting entirely and cut accounting disputes — barter beats pricing. THE CRITICAL LIMIT: even here onward transfer is restricted — in the Sea Lead/Turkon agreement the lessee may not sub-charter or assign space to a non-party carrier without written consent. So this is a closed club of qualified operators, not an open exchange. SHIPBUILDING BERTH SLOTS (figures are single-source or promotional — treat as directional, unlike the ocean mechanics above which are FMC-filing grade): slots carry acknowledged commercial value and scarcity is extreme, with one report saying Ultramax delivery slots are unavailable until at least 2029. But the premium is expressed in the SECONDHAND ASSET price, not in a traded slot: a VLCC resale has cleared roughly US$40m above a newbuild, about 30%, while the newbuilding price index moved only 0.45% over the first seven months of 2026 even as new orders rose 65%. Newbuild positions ('resales') do change hands pre-delivery, but bilaterally through brokers using novation and refund guarantees — a broker market, never a screen. That is the realistic shape of a transformer slot business.
findings.figures: ONE/Evergreen transpacific slot-exchange agreement filed with FMC; ZIM/CSCL agreement sets round-voyage TEU allocations per trade; Sea Lead/Turkon bars sub-charter or assignment to a non-party carrier without written consent; VLCC resale clearing ~US$40m (~30%) above newbuild; newbuilding price index +0.45% over first 7 months of 2026 against new orders +65%; Ultramax delivery slots unavailable until at least 2029
findings.as_of: Shipbuilding price/order data covers first 7 months of 2026; FMC agreements and slot-charter trade press 2026. Shipbuilding figures are single-research-house or vendor sourced

findings.question: GPU/compute analogue: is anyone running a capacity-reservation exchange, and which way does the business model evolve?
findings.answer: Yes, and the direction of travel is the single most actionable analogue we have. Compute Exchange Inc. began as a procurement marketplace for RESERVED GPU CAPACITY across more than 100 providers, with buyer requests ranging from hundreds to tens of thousands of GPUs, and on 17 July 2026 it launched a SEPARATE marketplace for used and refurbished GPUs. The sequence matters: the capacity-reservation venue added a physical-asset venue, not the reverse. That says a forward/slot venue needs a spot leg alongside it to be useful — which both validates Anza's physical-listings structure and argues a transformer slot desk must carry both legs from day one rather than launching as a pure forward market. PRICING OPACITY is the operating reality and the arbitrage: Compute Exchange's indicative Q3 2026 used H100 ranges are $16,000-$20,000 (PCIe) and $22,000-$27,000 (SXM5), while vendor-published estimates for the same part span roughly $6,000 to $28,000 — about a 4.7x spread across sources, i.e. no price discovery. One vendor estimates ~400,000 H100s will trade secondhand in 2026 at roughly $12-15bn, but that is unverified and from an interested party. WARRANTY IS THE RECURRING FRICTION, and it maps directly onto transformers: warranty rights generally stay with the ORIGINAL purchaser, and third parties sell replacement coverage at roughly 8-12% of purchase price per year. For a transformer, OEM warranty plus factory-test traceability is a large share of the asset's value and does not automatically travel with a resold unit or a novated order — so warranty/test-continuity is a product to sell, not just a risk to disclose. Caveat: most price sources here are GPU dealers or resale-service vendors with a commercial interest.
findings.figures: Compute Exchange: 100+ capacity providers, requests from hundreds to tens of thousands of GPUs, used/refurb marketplace launched 17 Jul 2026; indicative Q3 2026 used H100 $16,000-$20,000 (PCIe) and $22,000-$27,000 (SXM5) vs cross-vendor range ~$6,000-$28,000 (~4.7x spread); ~400,000 H100s / $12-15bn secondhand in 2026 (unverified vendor estimate); A100 prices projected to fall a further 10-15% through 2026; third-party warranty ~8-12% of purchase price per year
findings.as_of: Compute Exchange launch 17 Jul 2026; price ranges Q3 2026; depreciation projections through 2026

implication_for_business:
BUILD A BROKERED, CONSENT-MEDIATED ORDER-POSITION DESK WITH A PHYSICAL-EQUIPMENT LEG — NOT AN EXCHANGE — AND DO NOT UNDERWRITE A PERMANENT SHORTAGE.

Three sourced facts set the design. (1) The underlying is real: slots already exist as a priced primary instrument. GE Vernova books them explicitly (Q1 2026: 21 GW of agreements, only 2 GW firm, 19 GW reservations; reserved book 43 to 56 GW in one quarter; transformer slots booked through 2031), deposits run 10-30% of equipment cost and are typically non-refundable, and developers are already buying slots speculatively with no project attached — meaning holders of unwanted positions already exist. (2) But every purchase-order term I examined makes transfer contingent on the manufacturer's written consent, treats unapproved assignment as void, and prices consent at the OEM's discretion ($10,000 assignment fee in one Virginia Transformer form, with a reserved right to refuse outright). Moving a slot is a novation, not an assignment, so OEM consent is structurally unavoidable. The OEM — not the two counterparties — is therefore the gatekeeper and holds the pricing power. The first commercial act of this business is an OEM-side novation protocol with a handful of manufacturers, not a marketplace launch. (3) Every working analogue converges on the same shape. Ocean slot charter is the one functioning slot market and it works only because the unit is standardised (TEU on a named voyage), the counterparties are peers in a repeated game who both buy and sell, and there is a public FMC filing regime — and even there, assignment to a non-party requires written consent, i.e. a closed club, not an open exchange. Shipbuilding slots change hands only bilaterally through brokers via novation and refund guarantees, with the scarcity premium showing up in the secondhand asset price (VLCC resales ~US$40m / ~30% over newbuild) rather than in any traded slot. Wafer capacity reservation agreements have been financeable, amortisable and SEC-audited for 25+ years (Cirrus/GlobalFoundries: $60m non-refundable fee plus $195m prepayment, amortised to $6.7m/$14.7m by March 2026) and still do not trade. The binding constraint everywhere is fungibility, not instrument design: a 345kV GSU slot at a named factory under a named test regime is not interchangeable with another. That kills clearing and anonymous matching, but leaves brokerage, standardised novation documentation, escrow, valuation marks and provenance/compliance fully intact as fee businesses.

COMPETITIVELY there is genuine white space, with caveats. Anza Exchange is a new-equipment listings venue for physical units (transformers, HV breakers, modules) with free listings — it is not a slot venue and does not appear to transact order positions; its parent is PE-backed (Angeleno Group, Energy Capital Partners; the Munich Re premise is false). The surplus incumbents — Surplus Record (4,469 transformer listings, >5,000 inquiries/yr), Transformer Exchange, Utility Surplus Exchange, Electrical Trader — monetise attention or inventory, never the transaction or the time dimension. No named pure-play expediting or order-position desk surfaced; procurement advisory currently lives inside EPC/OE relationships (Burns & McDonnell / 1898 & Co.) and lead-time intelligence is already free lead-gen content from firms like Terrapin, so an information product alone has no moat. Compute Exchange shows the viable sequence — launch as a reserved-capacity procurement marketplace across many providers, then add the physical-asset leg (July 2026) — and its warranty problem names the adjacent product: rights stay with the original purchaser and third-party cover sells at 8-12%/yr, so warranty and factory-test traceability continuity, plus FEOC/origin compliance (sharply more valuable if the EO 14421 / DOE rulemaking claim verifies), are the services to sell around each transfer. Finally, price the window honestly: Rystad expects ~200 GVA of new transformer capacity online in 2026, so model the arbitrage as 3-5 years and make the durable revenue documentation, advisory and compliance rather than spread capture. Immediate diligence priorities before any plan is final: pull current assignment/novation terms from Hitachi Energy, Siemens Energy, GE Vernova, Prolec GE and WEG; establish whether a resale premium above contract price is enforceable or must be shared with the OEM; verify EO 14421 in the Federal Register; and verify Anza Exchange's actual scope, volumes and fees on-site.

topic: Demand side and regulatory state for large-load / data-centre grid interconnection as of 16 November 2026 — diligence for a transformer production-slot exchange & advisory business

findings.question: ERCOT Batch Zero: what is the status of the process after Abbott's early-August 2026 audit directive, and is it still paused?
findings.answer: The process is alive but frozen at a conditional stage. PUCT approved the Batch Zero framework on 18 June 2026. Abbott's letter of 3 August 2026 directed PUCT/ERCOT to audit data-centre projects in the queue; ERCOT suspended the Batch Zero Large Load classification notifications that had been scheduled for 7 August 2026 and paused classification and study activity. ERCOT then issued Batch Zero Verification Requests for Information and ran two audit tracks: a Batch Zero Audit covering all large loads, and a separate Community Impact Audit for computational loads of 25 MW and above. Every classification ERCOT has issued is explicitly CONDITIONAL. ERCOT has also paused authorising energisation of new large-load data centres and crypto-mining facilities until verification completes. ERCOT plans to file both the eligibility verification report and the community impact report on 10 December 2026 and to discuss them with PUCT at the 17 December 2026 open meeting. One secondary outlet reports ERCOT told PUCT on 5 November 2026 that reviewers and outside counsel had worked through first-round responses from 257 data-centre developers covering ~5,140 questions. I found no source confirming the energisation pause has been lifted, so treat it as still in force. One source says ERCOT expects to miss the original 9 April 2027 Batch Zero study-report date.
findings.figures: PUCT approval 18 Jun 2026; Abbott letter 3 Aug 2026; classification notices suspended 7 Aug 2026; Community Impact Audit threshold 25 MW; conditional classifications issued from 3 Sep 2026; 257 developers / ~5,140 questions (reported 5 Nov 2026, unverified); reports due 10 Dec 2026; PUCT open meeting 17 Dec 2026; original study report due 9 Apr 2027
findings.as_of: 2026-11-05 (latest datapoint); process status as of 2026-11-16

findings.question: What did the PUCT decide at or after its 20 August 2026 open meeting?
findings.answer: NOT CLEANLY ESTABLISHED, and sources conflict. ERCOT said it would seek a good-cause exception at the 20 August 2026 open meeting to suspend the Batch Zero classification timeline, and ERCOT filed a Batch Zero Verification and Audit presentation into PUCT Project 59142 that day (PUCT Interchange filing receipt timestamped 2026-08-20 09:01:26). Pillsbury reports that PUCT approved allowing ERCOT to continue processing large-load projects while conducting the Governor-directed verification and audit. Utility Dive and other trackers instead describe new data-centre connections as remaining paused. These are reconcilable — administrative processing continues while energisation authorisation is suspended — but I could not confirm the actual vote or order text from a primary PUCT document. Anyone relying on this should pull Project 59142 directly.

findings.question: How big is the ERCOT large-load queue in GW, what share is data centres, and have projects actually been culled?
findings.answer: Yes — a very large cull has already happened on paper, but it is a reclassification into a later batch rather than confirmed cancellation. Headline queue: ~474 GW of large-load interconnection requests, of which ERCOT reported 420,812 MW (90.2%) as data centres as of June 2026; Abbott's letter cited ~474 GW as more than 5x Texas record peak with ~90% of new power requests from data centres. ERCOT's 11 September 2026 Batch Zero update: ~735 projects total; roughly 373 projects carrying 302.2 GW placed OUTSIDE Batch Zero (deferred to Batch 1), and ~192–194 GW conditionally eligible — split into ~66 GW across 204 projects classified as base load and ~125–128 GW across 158 projects classified as studied load. ERCOT's own slides show both 125.4 GW and 127.9 GW for the studied-load figure, so the conditional total is either 191.8 or 194.3 GW. A pre-audit screen removed 315 projects / ~274 GW for lacking required studies. Importantly, ERCOT has NOT published a data-centre share of the retained ~192 GW. ERCOT has stated loads that fail verification or do not respond will be disqualified from Batch Zero; final disqualification numbers arrive with the 10 December report. One analyst expects only low-single-digit GW of further removals. BNEF warned the audit could delay 49.8 GW of data-centre load and cost projects up to $15bn.
findings.figures: ~474 GW queue; 420,812 MW (90.2%) data centres (Jun 2026); ~735 projects; 373 projects / 302.2 GW excluded from Batch Zero; conditional 191.8–194.3 GW = 66 GW base load (204 projects) + 125.4–127.9 GW studied load (158 projects); pre-audit screen 315 projects / ~274 GW; 198 GW of large load applied in Q1 2026 alone; BNEF: 49.8 GW delayed, up to $15bn cost; ERCOT-wide generation-queue withdrawals in a late-Jun/early-Jul 2026 window: 3.36 GW / 16 projects
findings.as_of: 2026-09-11 (ERCOT update); queue composition Jun 2026 — possibly stale

findings.question: Does ERCOT's Batch Zero eligibility test actually require proof of long-lead equipment orders such as transformers?
findings.answer: Yes — and this is the single most commercially relevant finding for a transformer-slot business. ERCOT's own 20 August 2026 PUCT presentation lists Batch Zero Eligibility Verification Supporting Documents including long-lead equipment attestations, purchase orders and delivery schedules; a retail service agreement is required if the developer is also the end-use customer. Depending on project status ERCOT may require evidence that transmission providers have purchased equipment such as transformers and breakers, proof site preparation/construction has begun, and purchase orders for customer-owned electrical equipment. 'Long-lead equipment' is defined as 18 months or more, and one guide states Batch Zero eligibility gates required equipment with 18-month-plus lead times to be ordered by the deadline. Per a law-firm summary, proof travels through the connecting utility rather than directly to ERCOT. One commentary (consultant blog, treat as secondary) claims the recurring deficiency ERCOT is finding is the inability to establish that equipment has been ordered and will be delivered before energisation. Sources disagree on the attestation deadline (15 July vs 24 July 2026), so verify against the PGRR 144/145 text.
findings.figures: Long-lead equipment threshold: 18 months; attestation deadline reported as 15 Jul 2026 or 24 Jul 2026 (conflicting); documents required: long-lead equipment attestations, POs, delivery schedules, land/real-estate agreements, end-user agreements

findings.question: FERC's six Section 206 show-cause proceedings against PJM, CAISO, MISO, NYISO, ISO-NE and SPP: what did the RTOs file, were any held in abeyance, and has FERC acted?
findings.answer: Partially established, and the critical dates land on TODAY. FERC issued six parallel §206 show-cause orders on 18 June 2026 — one each to PJM, MISO, SPP, CAISO, ISO-NE and NYISO — preliminarily finding existing tariffs may be unjust and unreasonable for lacking clear large-load and co-located-load provisions. Dockets: PJM EL26-67 (195 FERC ¶ 61,211), SPP EL26-68 (195 FERC ¶ 61,213), running through EL26-72. Original responses were due 17 August 2026 (60 days). The orders permitted abeyance of up to 90 days. ABEYANCE: secondary trackers report all six obtained abeyance on 14 August 2026, pushing responses to 16 November 2026 (SPP reportedly 20 November) with answers due 16 December 2026 — I could NOT verify this against a primary FERC document, so treat the exact dates as unverified. FERC HAS acted procedurally at least once: a FERC order at 196 FERC ¶ 61,214 in Docket EL26-67-001 dated 21 September 2026 is posted on PJM's site, but the proxy blocked the fetch so its content is not established. WHAT THE RTOs FILED: not established as filed. CAISO was fast-tracking its Large Loads Stakeholder Initiative toward a 16 November 2026 compliance filing; MISO's cost-recovery terms were expected in its 16 November response and American Municipal Power opposed MISO's abeyance motion; ISO-NE was reportedly proposing a 'bring your own generation' obligation; NYISO and ISO-NE are described as earliest-stage with no tariff revisions proposed. SPP is seen as furthest ahead because FERC approved its High Impact Large Load (HILL) process in January 2026, cited in the orders as a possible model. PJM's co-location issues run in a separate docket, EL25-49. No FERC merits ruling resolving any of the six proceedings has been found.
findings.figures: Orders issued 18 Jun 2026; 6 proceedings; dockets EL26-67 to EL26-72 (+ EL25-49 for PJM co-location); original response 17 Aug 2026; abeyance up to 90 days, reportedly granted 14 Aug 2026; responses reportedly due 16 Nov 2026 (SPP 20 Nov), answers 16 Dec 2026; order 196 FERC ¶ 61,214 in EL26-67-001 dated 21 Sep 2026; SPP HILL approved Jan 2026
findings.as_of: 2026-11-14 (latest secondary tracker); filings due 2026-11-16 — verify FERC eLibrary today

findings.question: NERC Computational Load Entity registration: did the Board approve it, was it filed with FERC, and what is its current status?
findings.answer: Yes, and EARLIER than the 5 December 2026 target — the premise is out of date in two ways. (1) The NERC Board of Trustees approved the Rules of Procedure revisions on 8 OCTOBER 2026, not December. (2) The single 'Computational Load Entity' concept was SPLIT, at NERC's 19 August 2026 posting, into two functional entity types: Computational Load Owner (CLO) and Computational Load Operator (CLOP); NERC's revised petition no longer defines 'computational load'. (3) NERC filed with FERC on 21 OCTOBER 2026 in Docket RR27-1-000 — ten weeks ahead of the 31 December 2026 deadline — and requested expedited action. The Board also authorised expedited procedures under ROP Section 1606 to develop a Section 1600 data request for registration, pending FERC approval. Registry thresholds were RAISED during drafting from 20 MW / 60 kV to 50 MW / 100 kV after stakeholder comment — a material narrowing of scope. The underlying mandate is FERC's 16 July 2026 order (Docket RD26-7-000), which required ROP/registry revisions by 31 December 2026 and a detailed informational workplan by 1 March 2027. Separately, the CLO-001 to CLO-003 Reliability Standards passed final ballot in October 2026 and advanced to Board review, with existing sites reportedly given 36 months to install disturbance recorders. CURRENT STATUS: FERC approval of RR27-1-000 is NOT ESTABLISHED as of today; the changes are not yet in force. Registration of qualifying entities is expected to begin in 2027, with further standards development during 2027 and mandatory compliance only after FERC approval.
findings.figures: Board approval 8 Oct 2026; FERC petition 21 Oct 2026, Docket RR27-1-000, expedited action requested; FERC mandate order 16 Jul 2026 (RD26-7-000); ROP deadline 31 Dec 2026; workplan due 1 Mar 2027; thresholds raised 20 MW/60 kV → 50 MW/100 kV; two new entity types (CLO, CLOP); CLO-001–003 passed final ballot Oct 2026; 36-month disturbance-recorder window for existing sites; registration from 2027

findings.question: How much data-centre capacity has actually been cancelled or deferred in 2026?
findings.answer: Real but contested, and the headline number is widely misused. The most-cited primary dataset is Sightline Climate's: ~140 US projects with 2026 opening dates totalling ~16 GW, of which only ~5 GW was under construction; Sightline estimates 30–50% of that capacity will slip or be dropped. An earlier Bloomberg-cited figure put the pipeline at 12 GW. This is the source of the 'nearly half of 2026 US data centres cancelled or delayed' headline. SemiAnalysis pushes back hard: most of what gets labelled 'cancelled' was speculative capacity that never had site control, financing or an interconnection agreement, while projects with those gates intact are on schedule. Named cases: Microsoft reportedly walked away from ~2 GW of new projects in the US and Europe (TD Cowen attributing it partly to oversupply); Oracle and OpenAI ended plans to expand the Abilene, Texas campus. Heatmap Pro counts at least $260bn of data-centre investment cancelled after local opposition in 2026 through early October, with local-opposition cancellations rising from 6 in 2024 to at least 25 in 2025. Wood Mackenzie reported developers added only 25 GW to pipelines in Q4 2025, half the prior quarter's pace, with only about a third of the pipeline under active development. Most of these figures reach me via secondary aggregators rather than the original Sightline or Bloomberg reports.
findings.figures: ~140 projects / ~16 GW with 2026 dates, ~5 GW under construction; 30–50% expected to slip or drop; ~7 GW reported delayed/cancelled on power constraints; Microsoft ~2 GW walked away; ≥$260bn cancelled on local opposition in 2026 to early Oct; local-opposition cancellations 6 (2024) → ≥25 (2025); Q4 2025 pipeline additions 25 GW, half prior quarter; ~1/3 of pipeline under active development

findings.question: Is anyone reporting freed-up transformer slots or resold interconnection positions as a result of cancellations?
findings.answer: NOT ESTABLISHED for transformers — this is the weakest link in the business thesis and I want to flag it plainly. I found no reporting of a secondary market, broker or exchange for transformer production slots freed by cancelled data-centre projects, and no pricing data for such trades. The three closest datapoints: (1) a single channel-check observation that some GAS TURBINE orders were being cancelled and slots sold, with customers switching to Bloom — the author was unsure whether it was a one-off; (2) SecondBloom Auctions launched a practice selling stranded data-centre EQUIPMENT for lenders, developers and estates — a resale channel for physical kit, not for factory slots; (3) procurement guides mention 'secondary-market qualification' as a risk-reduction option without describing any trading venue. On INTERCONNECTION positions the evidence runs against transferability: a November 2026 analysis of MISO's public project feed counts 2,325 withdrawn requests but only 17 pending transfers, and notes operators prohibiting or heavily restricting transfer of queue positions and agreements, leaving value trapped with the original applicant. Commercial advice to negotiate a transferability clause into the ISA is just that — advice, not a regulatory entitlement. ERCOT Batch Zero position transferability specifically: not established; needs a direct read of PGRR 144/145 and PUCT Project 59142. One adjacent reuse example: Portland General Electric freed 80 MW of interconnection headroom via load modelling — capacity recovery, not a cancelled-project transfer. Note also the structural logic problem: SemiAnalysis's point is that the projects being cancelled are largely the ones that never ordered long-lead equipment, so they may have no slots to resell.
findings.figures: MISO (counted Nov 2026): 2,325 withdrawn requests vs 17 pending transfers; PGE freed 80 MW headroom; no slot-resale price data found; no broker/exchange identified

findings.question: What is the current state of transformer lead times, slot reservations and factory capacity — i.e. is the scarcity an exchange would monetise actually tightening or easing?
findings.answer: Tight but easing at the margin, and the scarcity looks more like allocation/sequence scarcity than absolute capacity scarcity. Lead times: the most consistent figure is ~128 weeks average order-to-delivery for large power transformers and ~143 weeks for generator step-up units, and that survey figure was DOWN 10 WEEKS quarter-on-quarter. Other ranges: 110 to 160+ weeks for LPTs, 144 to 210 weeks for GSUs; a DOE-funded national lab cited at up to 4 years standard and 5 years custom; a July 2026 national-lab summary gives ~2.5–3 years for a typical 100 MVA LPT; one outlook expects stabilisation near 30–36 months through 2027 as Siemens Energy, Hitachi Energy and GE Vernova ramp. Bushings are flagged as the longest-lead component at up to 130 weeks; medium-voltage switchgear 52–80 weeks. SLOT ECONOMY: manufacturers typically hold a production slot for 10–30% of equipment cost, with the reservation amount at risk if no order follows. GE Vernova's Q1 2026 gas-equipment book was 21 GW of agreements of which only 2 GW were FIRM orders and 19 GW were reservations — reservations are displacing firm orders. One April 2026 Korean-language report says GE Vernova transformer slot reservations are secured through 2031 (flag as possibly stale and translation-dependent). Data-centre operators are reported to be securing slots years ahead or paying premiums, pricing out non-data-centre buyers. CRITICAL COUNTERPOINT: global large-power-transformer factory utilisation is put near 70% in 2026, modelled to reach 80% by 2030. Backlogs are at records — Siemens Energy Grid Technologies €51bn order backlog (August 2026); GE Vernova's buyout of the remaining 50% of Prolec GE added ~$5bn of backlog; Hitachi Energy committed CAD 479m to transformer insulation manufacturing in London, Ontario, completing by 2028 (a materials project, not finished units). implication_for_business:
BOTTOM LINE: the ADVISORY leg of the business is validated and has an unusually sharp, time-boxed demand window right now; the EXCHANGE leg is not validated by any evidence I could find and rests on an assumption that contradicts the best available reasoning about which projects are being cancelled.

1) The strongest demand signal is regulatory, not commercial. ERCOT's Batch Zero eligibility verification requires long-lead equipment attestations, purchase orders and delivery schedules, with "long-lead" defined as 18+ months — squarely the transformer window. Every Batch Zero classification ERCOT has issued is CONDITIONAL, and ERCOT has said loads that fail verification or fail to respond will be disqualified. That converts a transformer slot from a procurement item into a COMPLIANCE ASSET: evidence needed to keep a grid position worth hundreds of MW. Plan the first product as attestation/evidence packaging and slot-documentation diligence, not as a trading venue. Pricing anchor: BNEF put the audit's exposure at 49.8 GW of delayed load and up to $15bn of project cost.

2) The revenue window is front-loaded into the next 60 days and is datable. 16 Nov 2026 (TODAY) — five RTO show-cause responses due in EL26-67/69/70/71/72; 20 Nov — SPP; 10 Dec — ERCOT files its Batch Zero verification and community-impact reports; 16 Dec — FERC answers due; 17 Dec — PUCT open meeting on the ERCOT reports; 31 Dec — FERC's deadline for NERC ROP revisions (already met early, 21 Oct, in RR27-1-000); 1 Mar 2027 — NERC workplan; 2027 — CLO/CLOP registration begins. Build the go-to-market calendar on these dates. Also note the premise correction: the NERC step the original research expected on 5 Dec 2026 ALREADY HAPPENED on 8 Oct (Board) and 21 Oct (FERC filing), and the entity was split into Computational Load Owner and Operator with thresholds raised to 50 MW / 100 kV — so any plan written against "Computational Load Entity" and a December board date is stale.

3) Do not plan to trade interconnection positions. MISO's own feed shows 2,325 withdrawals against 17 pending transfers, and operators prohibit or heavily restrict transfer of queue positions and agreements. The tradable instrument is the factory slot (held by a forfeitable 10–30%-of-cost deposit, so there is a real economic interest capable of assignment), NOT the grid position. You cannot bundle the two, which removes the most valuable product you might have wanted to sell.

4. Two findings undercut a pure scarcity-arbitrage thesis and should be stress-tested before committing capital. First, scarcity is easing at the margin: the LPT survey figure fell 10 weeks quarter-on-quarter, and global LPT factory utilisation is put near 70% — if that is right, the bottleneck is ALLOCATION AND SEQUENCE, not tonnage, so an exchange monetises queue order, which is a thinner and more cyclical margin and erodes as Siemens, Hitachi and GE Vernova ramp. Second, and more serious: SemiAnalysis's argument is that the cancelled projects are overwhelmingly the speculative ones that never had site control, financing or interconnection — precisely the projects that never ordered long-lead equipment. If true, the cancellation wave generates NO sell-side slot inventory, and the exchange has nothing to list. I found zero reporting of freed transformer slots; the only slot-resale datapoint in existence is a single unconfirmed channel check about GAS TURBINES, and the only live resale business (SecondBloom Auctions) sells stranded physical equipment, not factory slots.

5) Recommended next diligence, in priority order: (a) confirm today's FERC filings in EL26-67 through EL26-72 directly in eLibrary — my abeyance dates (14 Aug 2026) and 16 Nov deadline come only from secondary trackers, and the one primary FERC order I located (196 FERC ¶ 61,214, EL26-67-001, 21 Sep 2026) could not be fetched; (b) read PGRR 144/145 and PUCT Project 59142 for whether a Batch Zero position or its equipment evidence can be assigned at all; (c) interview 3–5 transformer OEM sales desks on whether they permit assignment of a reserved slot to a third party, since if OEMs forbid novation the exchange is legally impossible regardless of demand; (d) get the primary Sightline Climate report rather than the aggregator write-ups. Note one environment limitation: direct page fetching failed (www.pjm.com did not resolve and would need allowing in the session's network settings), so every figure here is search-result sourced and no primary PDF was read end-to-end.

findings.question: What do third-party inspection (FAT witnessing) and expediting / factory-surveillance services actually cost?
findings.answer: Only one published day rate exists in the open web: Sinospect, a China-based inspection provider, lists USD 730 per witness-day for FAT witnessing, with planning, travel and reporting billed on top; it quotes engineering FATs to a client-specific protocol as a fixed price per job rather than per day. NOT ESTABLISHED: any independent day-rate survey, any major inspection body's published rate, regional rate differentials, or a per-order expediting fee benchmark. findings.question: What are owner's engineer and engineering-management scopes worth as a percentage of project cost?
findings.answer: The only authoritative figure is from MISO's Transmission Cost Estimation Guide (MTEP26 draft, presented to the Planning Subcommittee 11 March 2026): engineering, environmental studies, and testing and commissioning are estimated at 3% of project cost, and project management at 5.5% of project cost. These are planning-level allowances for cost categories, not owner's engineer fees as such, and they are the defensible number to anchor to. Weaker adjacent data points: a vendor article on gas-turbine EPC puts owner's engineer services at roughly USD 1M-4M on a plant and all owner's costs at 8-12% of EPC value; an industry blog puts substation protection-and-control design engineering at 8-15% of total project cost (P&C design only, not full owner's engineer). NOT ESTABLISHED: a true owner's-engineer-fee-as-%-of-project-cost benchmark for transmission or substation work. The MISO 3% + 5.5% = 8.5% soft-cost envelope is the most credible ceiling to reason from, and it is the budget line a slot-exchange fee would have to be carved out of.

findings.question: What do strategic sourcing / procurement advisory engagements and supply-chain risk retainers cost?
findings.answer: Three fee architectures are in use, all documented only by consultancies' own marketing (so directional, not independent). (1) GAINSHARE: 15-25% of documented first-year savings is the most frequently cited band, with a 12-24 month measurement window; a second source gives 10-30% for outcome/risk-share deals; a rate calculator shows 10% of first-year savings as an example; a purchasing consortium is quoted saying 25-50% of savings is 'commonplace' — treat that as a high outlier. Gainshare contracts must define the baseline and adjust for commodity index shifts, FX, volume and specification changes, with Finance approval — which is exactly the dispute surface a slot-exchange gainshare model would inherit. (2) PROJECT FEE: a single-category sourcing event runs USD 25,000-90,000 over 8-14 weeks; a multi-category wave of 5-10 categories runs USD 150,000-500,000 over 6-12 months. (3) RETAINER: USD 3,000-8,000/month for advisory-level input, USD 5,000-18,000/month for embedded operational leadership, and USD 5,000-25,000/month for procurement-focused retainers. NOT ESTABLISHED: any data-centre-specific or utility-specific sourcing fee benchmark; critical-equipment sourcing may price very differently from general indirect categories.

findings.question: What are brokerage and commission take rates for industrial capital equipment and for large-transaction intermediation?
findings.answer: Two distinct pricing regimes, and the gap between them is the central pricing decision for the business. SMALL/MID TICKET (machinery-broker regime): machinery brokers on consignment charge 5-15% of sale price, with heavy equipment typically 8-12%; independent industrial sales reps earn 5-12% of closed deal value across USD 5,000-500,000 deals, with large deals at the low end (a USD 200,000 capital equipment sale at 5% = USD 10,000); a published draft Equipment Brokerage Agreement sets commission at 10% of final sale price, due upon closing of the transaction. LARGE TICKET (advisory regime): the classic Lehman scale (5-4-3-2-1% on successive USD 1M tranches) yields USD 300,000 on a USD 20M transaction — a 1.5% effective rate; Double Lehman (10-8-6-4-2) yields USD 600,000, or 3.0%. Firmex data found the formula barely affects the outcome: average effective fees ran 4.8% at USD 5M falling to 1.9% at USD 150M. Middle-market success fees sit at roughly 2-5% of deal value, and about two-thirds of engagement letters carry a fixed minimum fee; Axial's 2026 data reportedly shows Lehman-style plus flat structures account for 79% of engagement letters. Equipment FINANCE brokerage is a separate business at 2-6% of funded amount (one source says 0.5-2%) — do not use it as a comparable. NOT ESTABLISHED: any observed take rate for scarce-capacity or slot intermediation specifically.

Lehman 5-4-3-2-1 = 1.5% effective on USD 20M; Double Lehman = 3.0%. Firmex effective fees 4.8% at USD 5M to 1.9% at USD 150M. Middle-market success fees 2-5%; ~2/3 carry a minimum fee; 79% of engagement letters Lehman-style or flat (Axial 2026). Equipment finance brokers 2-6% of funded amount.
