findings.question: Is escrow used, what does it cost, and who pays?
findings.answer: Escrow pricing is well documented in general commerce but sources conflict badly and none address industrial capital equipment. Dedicated online escrow providers charge roughly 0.89%-3.25% of transaction value, declining with size; Escrow.com's published tiers run 2.6% at the bottom, 1.9% for USD 50,000-200,000, falling to 0.95% above USD 3,000,000, with minimums that raise the effective rate on small deals. For genuinely large transactions the cited figures drop an order of magnitude: 0.10%-0.50% (calculator) and 0.20%-0.50% of transaction value for million-dollar deals, with the caveat that complex commercial deals fall outside that band. Who pays: typically split 50/50 between buyer and seller, or borne entirely by the buyer as a transaction expense — the escrow agreement must specify which. Commercial escrows add charges for bulk-sales compliance, extended holding periods and multi-lender coordination; wire and banking fees are separate. NOT ESTABLISHED: that escrow is customary practice in capital equipment order or slot transfers at all. No source shows escrow being used for an OEM order-position transfer. For a USD 5-10M slot transfer, a 0.20-0.50% escrow cost (USD 10,000-50,000) is the planning assumption, but it is an inference from general commercial escrow, not an observed transformer-market practice.
findings.figures: Online escrow 0.89%-3.25% of value. Escrow.com: 2.6% floor tier, 1.9% for USD 50k-200k, 0.95% above USD 3M. Large/commercial transactions 0.10%-0.50%; 0.20%-0.50% for million-dollar deals. Cost typically split 50/50 or paid wholly by buyer.
findings.as_of: 2025-2026; sources mutually inconsistent

findings.question: What do anti-assignment clauses and novation practice actually require, and do OEMs permit assignment with consent?
findings.answer: The mechanism is consent-gated and the OEM holds a veto. Standard anti-assignment language bars a party from assigning, delegating or transferring rights or obligations without the other party's prior written consent, with any attempt without consent 'deemed null and void.' Whether a non-consented transfer is void or merely a breach turns on whether the clause is drafted as a condition (void) or a covenant (breach only), and that varies by state — some statutes also limit restrictions on assigning payment rights. Assignment moves rights and the original party normally stays liable; novation substitutes a new contract, fully releases the original party, and requires every party's consent — the remaining counterparty can simply refuse, which blocks it. The best primary-source evidence of OEM practice found is GE Vernova's Terms of Purchase, Section 13 'Assignment, Subcontracting and Change of Control': written consent is required to transfer order rights or obligations 'including by change of ownership or control, by operation of law or otherwise,' and the assignee 'shall be bound by the terms and conditions of this Order.' The October 2025 US revision is the most commercially telling: consent may be granted 'contingent upon Buyer's qualifications review,' with prompt written notice required after assignment. The Europe Rev. A version adds a further-assurances duty to 'execute all documents as may be necessary to give effect to such assignment or novation' in good faith and in a timely manner at the counterparty's request. IMPORTANT CAVEAT: these are GE Vernova's terms as BUYER, not transformer OEM terms of sale — the clause structure is indicative, not directly applicable. NOT ESTABLISHED: Hitachi Energy, Siemens Energy or GE Vernova terms of SALE for transformers; no transformer OEM sale-side assignment clause was located, and no evidence either way on whether transformer OEMs in practice grant consent to a pure order-position resale to an unaffiliated buyer.
findings.figures: Standard clause: no transfer without prior written consent; unconsented attempt 'null and void.' GE Vernova Terms of Purchase Sec. 13 (Oct 2025 US rev.): consent 'contingent upon Buyer's qualifications review' + prompt written notice. Europe Rev. A: further-assurances duty to execute documents giving effect to 'such assignment or novation.' Novation requires unanimous consent; assignor generally remains liable under a mere assignment.
findings.as_of: GE Vernova terms Oct 2025 (purchase-side); general contract-law sources 2016-2026

findings.question: How are slot reservations structured, and does the OEM already capture the resale value of a defaulted slot?
findings.answer: Slot reservation agreements are a recognised, named instrument — 'slot reservation agreements' is GE Vernova's own term — and they are a paid option on future production: the customer converts to a firm order if the project proceeds, and if it does not, the manufacturer keeps the deposit AND resells the slot. That single mechanic is the most important competitive fact uncovered: the OEM is already the incumbent reallocator of distressed slots and already monetises default. The best primary-source terms are in Energy Vault's FY2026 Form 10-Q covering its 2G Energy arrangement: the reservation fee is 'generally non-refundable,' is credited toward milestone payments if a separate sales contract is signed by a deadline, and 'does not obligate either party to execute the sales contract'; the fee was increased from USD 10.0 million to USD 17.0 million by amendment with the sales-contract deadline extended. Scale and scarcity pricing at GE Vernova: 58 GW of a 122 GW total sits in slot reservations rather than firm orders; 11 GW of gas orders plus slot reservations were signed in a single quarter; H1 2026 orders were priced more than 20% above late-2025 orders; data centres take about a fifth of the gas turbine book. For transformers specifically, one aggregator estimates transformer and switchgear slot holds at 10-30% of equipment cost at land close — UNVERIFIED against any primary source. Critically, a reservation 'does not guarantee delivery or an operating date,' and the final purchase agreement and price are sometimes still open when the reservation is signed. NOT ESTABLISHED: any public transformer-specific slot agreement with a utility or data-centre operator; any observed resale or transfer of an OEM slot reservation at a premium between third parties. The secondary-market activity that IS documented is in used/refurbished turbines and jet engines (used turbines ~USD 1.5-1.7M/MW, refurbished ~USD 1.3M/MW per Origin Partners), not in slot transfers. One commentator forecasts that certified inspection, standardised refurbishment grades and dedicated brokers will emerge — a forecast, not a current fact. Note: open-factory.com, the one source treating slots as a transferable financial asset, could not be fetched — the host has to be allowed in the session's network settings.
findings.figures: Energy Vault FY2026 10-Q: reservation fee 'generally non-refundable,' raised from USD 10.0M to USD 17.0M by amendment; credited to milestone payments; no obligation to execute the sales contract. GE Vernova: 58 GW of 122 GW in slot reservations vs firm orders; 11 GW of orders + reservations in one quarter; H1 2026 pricing >20% above late 2025; data centres ~20% of gas turbine book. Transformer/switchgear slot holds 10-30% of equipment cost (unverified). Used turbines USD 1.5-1.7M/MW; refurbished ~USD 1.3M/MW.
findings.as_of: Energy Vault 10-Q period ended 30 June 2026; GE Vernova March 2026 conference; turbine secondary-market reporting 9 November 2026

findings.question: What are the deposit/milestone, liquidated damages and cancellation-charge structures on a transformer order?
findings.answer: PAYMENT STRUCTURE: commonly cited splits are 30/70, 10/80/10 and 20/70/10 across order confirmation, pre-shipment and post-commissioning. A 2026 EPC-oriented guide gives 15-30% advance payment, progress payments tied to verifiable production stages, final payment tied to FAT and shipment, and 5-10% retention held through commissioning. LIQUIDATED DAMAGES: delay LDs are charged daily or weekly against delivery milestones and typically capped at 5-15% of contract price; one worked example is 0.5% per week to a 5% maximum. A real utility bid — Greenville Utilities Commission RFB 26-18, opened 26 May 2026 — sets efficiency-loss damages by formula: Liquidated Damages = 2 x (Delivered TOC - Quoted TOC), with 30-day payment terms. CANCELLATION: the harshest documented seller-side term is MARS Transformers': if the buyer cancels other than for the seller's material breach, the seller recovers all costs and expenses incurred and commitments made PLUS an amount equal to the seller's expected profit on the order, or retains payments already made as liquidated damages. By contrast, Advanced Energy's buyer-side Terms of Purchase (Rev. 03/2026) subject any claim for cancellation charges to the buyer's 'reasonable approval.' The commercial consequence for a slot exchange: a cancelling buyer's downside is full cost plus the OEM's expected profit, which is precisely the loss a transfer is meant to avoid — that spread is the value the exchange captures. Most percentage figures here come from supplier marketing content and are not standardised; the GUC bid and the Advanced Energy terms are the primary sources.
findings.figures: Payment splits 30/70, 10/80/10, 20/70/10. EPC guide: 15-30% advance, 5-10% retention through commissioning. Delay LDs capped 5-15% of contract price; example 0.5%/week to 5% cap. GUC RFB 26-18 (26 May 2026): LD = 2 x (Delivered TOC - Quoted TOC); 30-day payment terms. MARS Transformers cancellation: all costs + commitments + seller's expected profit, or retention of payments as LDs. Advanced Energy Rev. 03/2026: cancellation charges subject to buyer's reasonable approval.
findings.as_of: GUC bid 26 May 2026; Advanced Energy terms Rev. 03/2026; supplier guidance undated

findings.question: Does warranty transfer on a resold new unit, and does an intermediating firm need a licence, bond or insurance in the US?
findings.answer: WARRANTY TRANSFERABILITY — NOT ESTABLISHED for power transformers. No power-transformer OEM warranty document was located. The general commercial pattern, inferred from lighting, HVAC and equipment analogues, is that non-transferable-to-original-purchaser-only is a common default (several vendors void coverage once the original purchaser ceases to own the product); where transfer is permitted it is commonly limited to the unused remainder of the original term; transfer typically requires affirmative registration and notice within a deadline (e.g. 90 days for Trane) and may carry a transfer fee; and relocation or modification can void coverage outright. Treat warranty continuity on a transferred order as an open contractual item to be negotiated into the novation, not an assumption. LICENSING — NOT ESTABLISHED for equipment intermediation specifically. There is no federal business broker licence. Where real property transfers, a real estate licence is generally required; roughly 12-17 states require some form of licence for business sales (sources conflict on the count and none is official), with California, Florida, Michigan, Nevada and South Dakota cited, Nevada also requiring a separate business broker permit, and Illinois using Secretary of State registration instead. Many states require nothing for asset-only sales (Texas is the cited example). No source addresses machinery or equipment brokerage. INFERENCE: pure sale-position intermediation that does not touch real property or transport-for-hire most likely needs no special licence, but a slot exchange that also arranges logistics would need to check the FMCSA regime, where freight brokers and forwarders must post a USD 75,000 bond (BMC-84, or a BMC-85 trust fund). INSURANCE — quantified: consultants average USD 62/month for professional liability, with annual policies from about USD 400 to over USD 3,750; USD 1M/USD 1M policies run USD 500-1,500/yr for consultants and USD 400-800 for solo practitioners under USD 100k revenue; technology/IT consultants run USD 1,200-3,500/yr (one guide says USD 1,500-7,500), and the single best data point is a 2026 vendor sample of 289 IT-firm quotes (May-October 2026, USD 1M limits) with a median Tech E&O premium of USD 3,032. Larger firms pay USD 5,000-15,000+. USD 1M is the minimum most client contracts require and USD 1M/USD 2M is the modal tier demanded by enterprise MSAs; add 15-40% in high-litigation states (California, New York, Florida, Cook County IL).

implication_for_business:
Five things fall out of this evidence that should shape the plan directly.

1. THE FEE HAS TO BE PRICED AGAINST A SOFT-COST BUDGET OF ROUGHLY 8.5%, NOT AGAINST THE EQUIPMENT PRICE. MISO's MTEP26 guide (the only authoritative benchmark found) allows 3% for engineering/environmental/testing-commissioning and 5.5% for project management. A slot-exchange fee competes for room inside that envelope. Within it, the credible pricing points are: Lehman-type effective rates of 1.5-3.0% on a USD 20M transaction, or 1.9-4.8% effective across USD 5M-150M per Firmex; machinery-broker norms of 5-15% (heavy equipment 8-12%) are almost certainly unsustainable at transformer ticket sizes and would price the service out. On a USD 5-10M transformer order, 1.5-3% is USD 75k-300k — comfortably above a FAT-witnessing business (USD 730/day) and comparable to a multi-category sourcing wave (USD 150k-500k). Expect buyers to demand a minimum fee structure: about two-thirds of advisory engagement letters carry one.

2. THE OEM IS NOT A NEUTRAL PARTY — IT IS THE INCUMBENT COMPETITOR. The single most consequential finding is that when a slot reservation lapses, the manufacturer keeps the deposit AND resells the slot. The OEM already captures 100% of the reallocation value and has no economic reason to bless a third-party exchange that transfers that value to the defaulting buyer. Energy Vault's 10-Q shows the OEM-side preference clearly: a non-refundable fee (raised USD 10.0M to USD 17.0M) that is credited only if a sales contract is signed by a deadline and that obligates neither party to sign. Any plan must have an explicit answer to 'why does the OEM cooperate' — most plausibly because OEM consent is conditioned on qualifications review of the assignee (GE Vernova's Oct 2025 language), and an exchange that pre-qualifies and credit-screens buyers reduces the OEM's own counterparty risk. That is the wedge: sell the OEM a vetted substitute buyer, not a secondary market.

3. CONSENT IS A VETO AND THAT MAKES THE EXCHANGE AN OPTION BROKER, NOT A TITLE HOUSE. Anti-assignment language renders unconsented transfers 'null and void,' and novation requires unanimous consent with the remaining counterparty free to refuse outright. The firm therefore cannot warehouse or take title to slot positions; it can only broker consent-conditional transfers, and every mandate must be contingent-fee with the OEM consent as the closing condition. Build the engagement letter around that, and budget legal cost per deal for a three-party novation, not a two-party assignment.

4. THE REAL VALUE SOLD IS AVOIDANCE OF A CANCELLATION CHARGE THAT EQUALS COST PLUS THE OEM'S EXPECTED PROFIT. MARS Transformers' terms — all costs and commitments plus the seller's expected profit, or forfeiture of payments as LDs — define the seller's walk-away loss. Combined with 15-30% advance payments and 5-10% retention, a buyer abandoning a slot is exposed to a large, substantially sunk amount. That exposure, not the lead-time saving, is the quantifiable willingness-to-pay for the distressed seller side. The buyer side's willingness-to-pay is separately anchored by observed scarcity pricing: GE Vernova's H1 2026 orders priced >20% above late 2025. Model the two sides separately; they pay for different things.

5. TWO ITEMS ARE OPEN RISKS THAT MUST BE RESOLVED BEFORE THE PLAN IS CREDIBLE, AND BOTH ARE CHEAP TO CLOSE. (a) Warranty transferability on a resold new unit is NOT ESTABLISHED for power transformers; the general default is original-purchaser-only, which if it holds materially degrades what the exchange is selling and must be negotiated into each novation. Obtain the warranty clauses from Hitachi Energy, Siemens Energy, GE Vernova and one or two tier-2 suppliers — their terms of SALE, which were not located. (b) Licensing for equipment intermediation is NOT ESTABLISHED; no federal business-broker licence exists and pure sale-position brokerage probably needs none, but any state where the firm touches real property, and the FMCSA USD 75,000 BMC-84 bond if it arranges transport-for-hire, need a counsel opinion. Operationally cheap: Tech/professional E&O at USD 1M/USD 2M (the modal enterprise MSA requirement) prices at a median of about USD 3,032/yr on 2026 quote data, call it USD 5,000-15,000 once revenue scales, plus 15-40% if domiciled in CA/NY/FL. Escrow, if used, costs 0.20-0.50% on million-dollar transactions, though no source shows escrow is actually customary in order-position transfers — do not assume it, and decide whether taking funds through escrow creates money-transmission or fiduciary exposure that a pure introduction model avoids.

One access note for the plan's source trail: open-factory.com — the one source that treats equipment slots as transferable financial assets, and the origin of the widely repeated '10-30% of equipment cost' transformer slot-hold figure — could not be fetched and would need to be allowed in the session's network settings. That figure remains unverified against any primary source and should not be used as a load-bearing assumption.
